title: Waste Collection Services in the US
one_liner: A mature essential-service industry where 2025 revenue growth came mainly from pricing, route density, acquisitions and specialty waste, while base collection volumes stayed soft.
overview: Waste Collection Services in the US remains an essential, route-based infrastructure industry tied to household formation, business activity, construction, industrial output and municipal outsourcing. The 2022 IBIS baseline put industry revenue at $68.0 billion, up 2.7% in 2022, with real revenue expected to reach about $71.4 billion by 2027. Updating that path with 2025 waste-collection producer prices implies an estimated 2025 nominal market near $85.0 billion, with roughly 6.0% nominal growth from 2024. The market is concentrated among vertically integrated haulers that own transfer stations, landfills, recycling assets and increasingly renewable natural gas or organics infrastructure, while smaller regional haulers compete on local contracts and specialized services.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn recurring fees from residential, commercial and industrial collection routes; roll-off container rental and pickup; transfer-station handling; landfill and disposal pass-throughs; recycling and commodity handling; municipal contracts; fuel and environmental recovery fees; and specialty waste services. Larger companies improve margins by internalizing collected tonnage into owned transfer stations and landfills, automating routes, raising contract yields and adding adjacent services such as medical waste, renewable natural gas, recycling processing and organics composting.

cost_structure.labor: High route labor, driver wages, benefits and training costs; public filings in 2025 cite wage inflation as a continuing cost pressure.
cost_structure.fuel_and_fleet: Collection trucks, containers, maintenance, tires, parts, insurance and fuel are core operating costs; automated side-loaders, CNG/RNG trucks and newer fleets require capital but can reduce labor and fuel intensity.
cost_structure.transfer_and_disposal: Third-party tipping fees, owned-landfill operating costs, transfer-station costs, closure/post-closure obligations and permitting costs are material; Republic said 67% of its collected solid-waste volume was disposed at landfills it owned or operated in both 2024 and 2025.
cost_structure.depreciation_and_capex: The business is capital intensive because trucks, carts, containers, compactors, transfer stations, landfills, recycling facilities and RNG projects must be replaced or expanded.
cost_structure.recycling_commodity_exposure: Recyclable commodity prices can lift or reduce revenue and margins; WM reported average single-stream recycled commodity prices declined about 20% in 2025 from 2024.
cost_structure.compliance: Environmental, safety, landfill, organics, hazardous-waste, stormwater, emissions and local-franchise rules raise administrative and operating costs.

current_dynamics: 2025-2026 industry conditions are favorable for revenue but uneven for volumes. Public haulers are still pushing contract yield above inflation, while residential collection and some roll-off/construction volumes remain pressured by municipal contract exits, softer construction activity and weaker discretionary commercial demand. Special waste, disaster cleanup, acquisitions, landfill internalization and pricing are offsetting weak base volumes. Recycling is strategically important but volatile because commodity prices fell in 2025, while organics, composting and RNG investments are expanding due to landfill-methane pressure and state diversion mandates.
whats_growing: Commercial and municipal contract pricing, with major operators reporting 2025 core price or yield gains in the 4%-6% range.
Special waste and disaster-related cleanup volumes, including 2025 wildfire remediation and hurricane recovery demand cited by Republic and WM.
Acquisition-driven scale, route density and vertical integration among national and regional haulers.
Medical waste and secure information destruction after WM’s November 2024 Stericycle acquisition.
Organics collection and composting infrastructure in states with landfill-diversion mandates, especially California.
Renewable natural gas and landfill-gas monetization projects tied to owned landfill networks.
whats_shrinking: Low-margin residential municipal contracts that large haulers are exiting or repricing.
Base collection volumes in some residential, large-container and transfer lines; Republic guided to about a 1.0% volume decline in 2026.
Recycling commodity revenue when fiber and single-stream prices weaken; WM reported about a 20% drop in average single-stream recycled commodity prices in 2025.
Small hauler expansion opportunities in markets where large operators control disposal assets and acquire regional players.
Traditional landfill disposal share in jurisdictions with stronger organics, packaging EPR and diversion rules.

2025-12-31: WM reported 2025 revenue of $25.204 billion, up 14.2%, with higher collection/disposal yield and Stericycle as key drivers.
2025-12-31: Republic reported 2025 revenue of $16.591 billion, up 3.5%, with 4.1% average yield offset by a 0.6% volume decline.
2026-02-11: GFL reported 2025 revenue of $6.616 billion and issued 2026 revenue guidance near $7.0 billion.
2026-05-01: California SB 54 permanent packaging EPR regulations became effective, increasing long-run pressure for recyclable and compostable packaging systems.
2026-06-18: Republic broke ground on the San Bernardino Sustainability Park, an organics facility expected to open in late 2026 with initial processing capability above 300,000 tons per year.
outlook: Through 2026, nominal revenue should keep growing as pricing, acquisitions and specialty waste offset muted base volumes. Margins should remain supported by route automation, landfill internalization, disciplined contract pricing and lower employee turnover, but labor, maintenance, insurance, fleet replacement, permitting and environmental compliance will remain persistent cost pressure. Longer term, the industry grows slowly in real terms because waste volumes track population, households, business formation and construction activity, while higher-value opportunities come from organics diversion, recycling quality, RNG, medical waste and vertically integrated disposal assets.

title: Waste Treatment & Disposal Services in the US
one_liner: A mature, regulated disposal industry where landfill scarcity, hazardous-waste compliance and renewable landfill-gas projects support pricing even when waste volumes soften.
overview: The industry covers NAICS 5622 establishments that operate waste treatment and disposal facilities, including hazardous-waste treatment and disposal, solid-waste landfills, waste combustors and other non-sewer disposal sites. The baseline IBIS file showed 2021 revenue of $21.6 billion and a 2021-2026 forecast of 1.2% CAGR to $22.9 billion, but Census Service Annual Survey data later placed 2022 NAICS 5622 revenue at $22.934 billion. Applying the broader Census Quarterly Services Survey trend for NAICS 562 through 2025 implies a 2025 NAICS 5622 market of about $27.3 billion, with 2025 growth near 3.9% and Q1 2026 broader-subsector revenue up about 0.5% year over year. Demand remains tied to consumer spending, construction, manufacturing output, industrial cleanup, medical and regulated waste, and storm or wildfire remediation. Pricing power is supported by high permitting barriers, limited landfill airspace, environmental compliance requirements and consolidation among vertically integrated national operators.

how_it_makes_money: Operators charge tipping fees, treatment fees, contract disposal fees and special-waste premiums based on waste type, volume, weight, distance, contamination risk and regulatory handling requirements. Hazardous-waste operators earn higher fees from industrial, healthcare, chemical, energy and remediation customers because handling requires permits, specialized equipment, manifests, incineration or stabilization capacity and environmental liability controls. Landfill operators earn gate fees from haulers and municipalities, internal disposal revenue from owned collection routes, special-waste revenue from construction, disaster cleanup and industrial streams, and ancillary revenue from transfer stations, leachate treatment, gas royalties, landfill-gas-to-energy and renewable natural gas. Waste-to-energy operators earn disposal fees plus electricity, steam, recovered metals and environmental-credit revenue where contracts and regulation support it.

cost_structure.capital_intensity: Medium to high; landfill airspace, incineration, TSDF capacity, RNG projects, trucks, monitoring systems and permits create high barriers to entry

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 operating environment is better for price than volume. Public company filings show landfill and collection yields continuing to rise, while residential and construction-related volumes are mixed and event-driven special waste from wildfires and hurricanes can temporarily lift landfill activity. Hazardous waste remains structurally attractive because disposal capacity is difficult to permit and industrial customers have fewer substitutes. At the same time, recycling and organics diversion cap long-run landfill tonnage growth, and lower recycled commodity prices can pressure adjacent recycling economics. PFAS regulation, landfill methane reporting updates and tighter emissions scrutiny are increasing compliance complexity, but they also create demand for specialized disposal, monitoring, remediation and consulting-backed waste services.

recent_developments: 2024-04-03: EPA signed GHGRP landfill reporting amendments updating methane modeling factors and collection-efficiency assumptions for MSW landfills.
2024-04-19: EPA finalized CERCLA hazardous-substance designation for PFOA and PFOS, increasing attention on PFAS handling, disposal and remediation liability.
2024-04-16: Covanta announced its rebrand to Reworld, repositioning the WTE operator around broader sustainable waste solutions.
2024-11-04: WM completed its $7.2 billion enterprise-value acquisition of Stericycle, expanding regulated medical waste and secure information destruction services.
2025-12-31: WM reported 2025 revenue of $25.204 billion, up 14.2%, with landfill volume gains and Stericycle acquisition contribution.
2026-06-11: Census QSS showed NAICS 562 revenue of $39.593 billion in Q1 2026, roughly flat year over year after strong 2025 revenue levels.
outlook: The industry should remain a low-to-mid single-digit grower through 2026, with revenue supported more by price, special-waste mix, hazardous-waste demand and renewable-gas monetization than by broad tonnage growth. Landfill airspace scarcity and permitting barriers protect incumbents, while methane, PFAS and groundwater rules raise compliance costs and favor firms with engineering, monitoring and balance-sheet capacity. The main downside risks are weak construction and industrial production, diversion mandates, lower recycling commodity prices, fuel and labor inflation, and political or community resistance to new disposal capacity. The most attractive pockets are hazardous waste, regulated medical waste, special waste, PFAS-related disposal, landfill gas/RNG, and integrated environmental solutions that bundle collection, transfer, disposal, remediation and reporting.
themes: Hazardous waste capacity as a moat
Landfill methane monitoring and RNG monetization
Special waste from disasters and remediation
Recycling diversion as both threat and adjacency
one_sentence: US waste treatment and disposal operators run landfills, hazardous-waste treatment facilities and waste-to-energy assets, earning mostly recurring tipping and service fees from municipalities, haulers, manufacturers, construction customers, healthcare providers and industrial waste generators.

title: Watch & Jewelry Repair
one_liner: Small, craft-based repair shops benefit when owners maintain watches and jewelry instead of replacing them, but growth is limited by scarce skilled labor and weak discretionary foot traffic.
overview: This industry covers establishments primarily providing repair and maintenance of watches, clocks and jewelry without primarily retailing new goods. Demand is tied to jewelry ownership, luxury and bridal purchases, household discretionary income, mall and main-street retail traffic, and the economics of repair versus replacement. The 2020 pandemic shock reduced foot traffic sharply, but the trade has since been supported by higher replacement costs, high gold prices, extended-service plans at chains, mail-in repair workflows and consumer interest in vintage, inherited and pre-owned luxury pieces.

current_dynamics: The industry is still dominated by small independent operators, but consumer expectations are shifting toward tracked, insured mail-in repair and faster status communication. High precious-metal prices make replacement more expensive, which can push owners toward repair, resizing and restoration, while also raising parts and scrap-metal costs. Jewelry retail traffic remains mixed as e-commerce gains share, but service counters and extended-service plans are valuable because repair work builds repeat visits and can carry better margins than merchandise sales. Skilled labor is the main constraint: BLS projected a 5% decline in jeweler employment from 2024 to 2034 even as replacement openings persist.

outlook: Revenue should grow slowly through 2026 rather than break out, with repair economics helped by high replacement costs, aging jewelry ownership, luxury resale and service-plan attachment. The best-positioned operators will be trusted specialists with insured handling, transparent estimates, appraisal capability and digital job tracking. The main risks are a shortage of skilled labor, volatile gold and parts costs, weaker discretionary spending, and competition from retailers that internalize repairs through centralized service centers.
one_sentence: The US watch and jewelry repair industry is a fragmented consumer-service trade centered on sizing, soldering, stone resetting, polishing, battery and strap work, appraisals, restoration and authorized watch servicing.

title: Water & Air Quality Testing Services
one_liner: Compliance-driven labs and field technicians test drinking water, wastewater, indoor air, ambient air and asbestos hazards for utilities, builders, industrial sites, public agencies and households.
overview: Operators collect samples, run lab analyses and issue compliance documentation for water contaminants, air pollutants, mold, asbestos, bacteria, heavy metals, pesticides, volatile organic compounds and other regulated substances. Demand is recurring because public water systems, construction projects, industrial facilities, food producers, property owners and municipalities must prove compliance with health, safety and environmental standards. The baseline 2021 mix was led by water quality testing at 52.1% of revenue, air quality testing at 34.0% and asbestos testing at 13.9%. By 2025, the strongest incremental demand is tied to PFAS drinking-water monitoring, lead service line inventories and replacement programs, tighter PM2.5 air-quality standards and continuing infrastructure spending.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from project-based and recurring fees for field sampling, laboratory analysis, chain-of-custody documentation, compliance reporting, building assessments, asbestos and mold inspections, drinking-water and wastewater testing, ambient and indoor air monitoring, and specialized contaminant panels such as PFAS, lead, mercury, nitrates, bacteria and VOCs. Larger firms also sell bundled inspection, certification, consulting and remediation-support services to utilities, industrial customers and public agencies.
cost_structure: The business is labor-heavy and compliance-heavy. In the 2021 baseline, wages were $2.942 billion, equal to about 43.7% of 2021 revenue, and profit was $606 million, equal to a 9.0% margin. Major nonlabor costs include lab supplies, sample containers, reagents, calibration gases, analytical instruments, vehicles, insurance, accreditation, software, data management and subcontracted specialty testing. 2025-2026 cost pressure is elevated for skilled technicians, chemists, certified industrial hygienists, QA staff and advanced PFAS instrumentation, while recurring compliance contracts help stabilize utilization.

Eurofins Environment Testing
SGS North America
Bureau Veritas
Intertek
Pace Analytical Services

Montrose Environmental Group
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions: higher regulatory testing demand and tighter customer budgets in interest-rate-sensitive construction and commercial real estate. Water testing is the strongest demand center because the 2024 PFAS drinking-water rule requires initial monitoring by 2027 and compliance by 2029, while the 2024 Lead and Copper Rule Improvements require more rigorous tap sampling, public inventories and lead service line replacement planning. Air testing demand is supported by the 2024 PM2.5 standard, industrial permitting, indoor-air concerns and wildfire-smoke exposure, but discretionary residential mold and air-quality tests are more cyclical. Public funding remains a major tailwind: EPA announced $6.2 billion in FY2025 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law water investments in October 2024 and $3.0 billion in new lead-reduction SRF funding in November 2025.
whats_growing: PFAS panels, lead and copper sampling, municipal service-line inventory support, drinking-water compliance monitoring, wastewater and emerging-contaminant testing, infrastructure-project environmental testing, indoor air quality work for schools and commercial buildings, ambient PM2.5 monitoring, and data/reporting services tied to public disclosure requirements.
whats_shrinking: Purely discretionary residential testing, lower-complexity commoditized pH and basic potability tests, legacy asbestos testing tied only to new product use, and construction-linked testing in private markets where 2025-2026 activity is pressured by higher financing costs. Asbestos work is not disappearing because older buildings still need abatement and renovation testing, but EPA's 2024 chrysotile asbestos rule reduces future new-use exposure over time.
recent_developments: 2024-02: EPA finalized a tighter annual PM2.5 air-quality standard, lowering the primary annual limit from 12.0 to 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter.
2024-03: EPA finalized a rule prohibiting ongoing uses of chrysotile asbestos, with phaseouts that affect future asbestos-related testing demand.
2024-04: EPA finalized the first national PFAS drinking-water limits, requiring initial monitoring by 2027 and compliance actions by 2029.
2024-10: EPA finalized Lead and Copper Rule Improvements requiring lead service line replacement within 10 years in most cases and more rigorous tap sampling.
2024-10: EPA announced $6.2 billion in FY2025 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law water-infrastructure investments through Clean Water and Drinking Water SRFs.
2025-11: EPA announced $3.0 billion in new state funding and $1.1 billion in redistributed unused funding to reduce lead in drinking water.
outlook: The industry outlook is positive but not explosive. Estimated 2025 revenue of about $7.5 billion leaves the market near the baseline 2026 projection of $7.7 billion, implying low- to mid-single-digit growth. Through 2026-2030, PFAS compliance deadlines, lead service line replacement programs, wastewater upgrades, PM2.5 implementation and aging public infrastructure should support recurring work. Private construction softness can cap near-term volume, but water-utility and public-sector mandates give the industry a steadier floor than many construction-adjacent services. Larger operators should keep gaining share where customers need multi-state coverage, accredited labs, rapid turnaround and defensible compliance reporting.
themes: Indoor air quality and mold risk

title: Wig & Hairpiece Manufacturing
one_liner: A small, fragmented US manufacturing niche serving fashion, cultural and medical hair-loss needs while competing against dominant low-cost imports.
overview: The industry manufactures wigs and hairpieces for aesthetic, cultural, religious and medical uses. The legacy 2021 baseline expected steady post-pandemic growth, but the current 2025 IBISWorld update shows the opposite: US revenue fell at a 2020-2025 CAGR of 3.9% to an estimated $161.8 million in 2025, with only 0.6% growth projected for 2025. Demand still benefits from aging, cancer-related and alopecia-related hair loss, higher disposable income for premium custom products and renewed male interest in modern hair systems, but domestic manufacturers remain squeezed by low-cost imports, tariff uncertainty, expensive human hair inputs and alternatives such as hair transplants, medications and minimalist natural-hair trends.

key_stats.market_size: $161.8 million in 2025; IBISWorld FAQ also lists $161.8 million for 2026
key_stats.businesses: 40 businesses in 2025, down at a 2020-2025 CAGR of 1.0%
key_stats.concentration: No company held more than 5% US industry share in 2025
key_stats.health_spending_driver: US national health expenditures were $5.3 trillion in 2024 and are projected by CMS to grow 5.4% annually over 2025-2034
key_stats.aging_driver: US population age 65+ rose from 55.6 million in 2020 to 64.6 million in 2025, a 16.2% increase
key_stats.disposable_income_driver: US disposable personal income was $22.866 trillion in 2025, up from $21.918 trillion in 2024

baseline_2022.market_size: $261.3 million in 2022, baseline-derived from the 2021 IBISWorld forecast path of $258.2 million in 2021 growing 1.2% annually to 2026
baseline_2022.wages: $53 million in 2021 baseline, equal to about 20.5% of 2021 revenue
baseline_2022.imports: $1.232 billion in 2021 baseline, equal to 83.8% of domestic demand
baseline_2022.exports: $19.6 million in 2021 baseline, equal to 7.6% of revenue

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by designing, sourcing hair or synthetic fibers, ventilating and assembling wigs, toupees, toppers, extensions and medical hair prostheses, then selling through salons, wig boutiques, medical channels, religious/cultural specialists, wholesale distributors, ecommerce and custom fitting services. Higher margins come from custom human-hair units, medical and cranial prosthesis work, lace-front and hand-tied construction, color matching, repairs and repeat replacement cycles.

cost_structure.labor: High-touch custom work is labor intensive; baseline wages were $53 million in 2021, about 20.5% of 2021 revenue.
cost_structure.materials: Human hair, synthetic fibers, lace, caps, adhesives, packaging and imported components are key variable costs; 2025 industry commentary cites rising raw-material expenses as a margin pressure.
cost_structure.profit: Baseline profit margin was 5.8% in 2021; current 2025 public IBISWorld page confirms financial benchmarks exist but does not disclose the 2025 margin publicly.
cost_structure.tariffs_and_imports: China-origin synthetic hair extensions under HTSUS 6704.19.0000 faced an additional 20% ad valorem China/Hong Kong duty effective March 4, 2025, on top of applicable Chapter 99 reporting and any Section 301 duties.
cost_structure.overhead: Rent, utilities, ecommerce, inventory holding, shipping, compliance, fitting rooms, marketing and returns are meaningful for firms with direct-to-consumer or salon-facing operations.

major_players: No company with more than 5% US industry share in 2025

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is smaller than the old baseline expected. Domestic demand is bifurcated: low-priced fashion wigs and extensions are largely import-led, while US operators defend niches in custom, medical, religious, premium human-hair and service-heavy fitting channels. Tariffs raise landed costs for China-origin goods but also increase uncertainty for firms that import fibers, finished wigs or components. Aging and healthcare spending support medical demand, while social media is reviving male hair systems, yet traditional wig demand is pressured by natural-hair acceptance, shaved-head preferences and hair-restoration substitutes.
whats_growing: Modern male hair systems and toupees, supported by 2025-2026 social-media visibility
Medical wigs and cranial prostheses tied to cancer treatment, alopecia and aging-related hair loss
Custom and premium human-hair units where fitting, color matching and service matter
Synthetic and blended products that offer lower price points and improved realism
Online discovery and direct-to-consumer replacement sales
whats_shrinking: Traditional mass-market domestic wig manufacturing exposed to import competition
Premium discretionary purchases among price-sensitive consumers facing high human-hair costs
Generic undifferentiated products that compete directly with China, Indonesia, Vietnam and Bangladesh sourcing
Male wig/toupee stigma-era products replaced by more natural-looking hair systems
Baseline-era growth expectations: the 2021 forecast pointed to $274.3 million by 2026, but the current public 2025-2026 figure is $161.8 million
recent_developments: Mar 2021: Baseline IBISWorld report estimated 2021 revenue at $258.2 million and projected $274.3 million by 2026.
Mar 4 2025: China/Hong Kong goods including HTSUS 6704.19.0000 became subject to an additional 20% ad valorem duty under the cited Chapter 99 provision.
Sep 11 2025: CBP ruling NY N352618 classified synthetic hair extensions under HTSUS 6704.19.0000 and confirmed no lower-duty exemption for the China-origin product in that ruling.
Nov 2025: IBISWorld updated the US industry report, estimating 2025 revenue at $161.8 million after a 2020-2025 CAGR decline of 3.9%.
Mar 26 2026: The Guardian reported a modern toupee and hair-system revival, including Aderans reporting a 43% 2025 increase in men buying hair systems.
Jun 2026: Census Vintage 2025 estimates showed the US 65+ population reached 64.6 million in 2025, up 16.2% from 2020.
outlook: The industry is likely to stabilize but not return quickly to the old 2021 forecast path. Growth opportunities are strongest in custom medical, religious, premium human-hair and men’s hair-system channels, especially where domestic providers bundle manufacturing with consultation, fitting, repair and replacement subscriptions. Headwinds remain significant: imports still dominate price-sensitive categories, tariffs can raise both finished-goods and input costs, and substitutes such as hair transplants, medications and natural-hair styling will keep a ceiling on traditional wig demand. A practical 2026 outlook is low growth from a reduced base, with margin upside only for differentiated operators that avoid commodity import competition.
